title: Nawaloka Hospitals’ Theja De Silva named Best CFO of the Year 2026 | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 21 October 2026 00:10
-     - 1

Nawaloka Hospitals PLC Group Chief Financial Officer Theja De Silva (right) receives award from CA Sri Lanka President Tishan Subasinghe

Nawaloka Hospitals PLC Group Chief Financial Officer Theja De Silva has been named Best CFO of the Year 2026 at the 47th National Conference of the Institute of Chartered Accountants of Sri Lanka (CA Sri Lanka), recognising his contribution to financial leadership and business transformation.

For De Silva, the recognition marks an important milestone in a career shaped by navigating challenging business environments and a belief that financial leadership goes far beyond managing numbers.

His professional journey includes working with organisations facing financial and operational difficulties, experiences that helped shape his approach to business recovery, governance and sustainable growth. Today, at Nawaloka Hospitals PLC, he has played a key role in strengthening financial discipline and contributing to the Group's financial turnaround, while supporting continued investment in healthcare services and innovation.

Reflecting on his leadership philosophy, De Silva said, "The true strength of a CFO lies not merely in understanding numbers, but in translating financial knowledge into sound decisions, inspiring people and creating opportunities for progress. Finance should not simply explain business performance after the event; it should help shape an organisation's future."

Holding professional qualifications including ACCA, FCPM and MSLID, De Silva also serves as Secretary of AAT Sri Lanka, extending his contribution beyond corporate leadership to the development of the accounting and finance profession. He is particularly passionate about encouraging young professionals to look beyond traditional accounting roles and embrace opportunities in strategic business leadership.

He attributes his professional growth to four essential pillars: knowledge, experience, soft skills and networking, believing that a combination of these qualities is fundamental to effective leadership.

De Silva expressed his gratitude to Nawaloka Hospitals Chairman Dr. H. K. Jayantha Dharmadasa, Deputy Chairperson Anisha Dharmadasa, the Board of Directors and his colleagues for their continued trust and support.

He hopes the recognition will inspire emerging finance professionals to pursue excellence with integrity, sound judgement and a commitment to making a meaningful difference.

title: “CNCI Achiever Awards 2026” celebrates 25th anniversary | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 21 October 2026 00:07
-     - 3

Industry and Entrepreneurship Development Deputy Minister Chathuranga Abeysinghe

CNCI Chairman Pradeep Kahawalage

The Ceylon National Chamber of Industries (CNCI), Sri Lanka’s premier industrial chamber, hosted the prestigious “CNCI Achiever Awards 2026” at Cinnamon Life, City of Dreams, Colombo, on 15 October, 2026 in collaboration with the Ministry of Industries and Entrepreneurship Development.

The annual flagship event recognises and rewards outstanding Sri Lankan industrialists for their remarkable achievements and excellence across the manufacturing and service sectors. A total of 129 Gold, Silver, Bronze, and Merit awards were presented across Extra Large, Large, Medium, Small, and Micro categories, recognising excellence at both provincial and district levels.

The event brought together a distinguished gathering of over 500 participants, including leading corporate industrialists, senior government officials, foreign ambassadors, diplomats, and sector representatives.

Industry and Entrepreneurship Development Deputy Minister Chathuranga Abeysinghe attended the grand occasion as the Chief Guest.

Addressing the gathering, Abeysinghe highlighted the vital role of emerging businesses in shaping the nation’s economic future. "A micro-level enterprise of today can become a giant business in a few years if it progresses on the correct track," said Abeysinghe.

He assured attendees that the government will rapidly implement new initiatives to support Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) with expansion, innovation, and entry into new markets. He added that the CNCI remains a critical partner in fostering an enabling environment, particularly for the SME sector.

Welcoming the guests, CNCI Chairman Pradeep Kahawalage emphasised the perseverance behind Sri Lanka›s industrial success. "Behind every award presented tonight is a story of resilience—small workshops that grew into national giants, and local innovators who became global pioneers. Their success stories are the true legacy of CNCI," Kahawalage noted, while thanking the CNCI team for their continuous efforts in raising domestic standards to international heights.

CNCI Deputy Chairman and the Chairman Internal Panel of Judges  Amila Sugathapala presenting the evaluation process, highlighted that the “Application to this award go through a very stringent judging process covering 14 areas and consist of an Internal and External Panel, led by the Vice Chancellor of the University of Sri Jayewardenepura and ably assisted by officials of key government and private institutions.”

The proceedings concluded with the Vote of Thanks delivered by CNCI Secretary General Major General (Retd.) Samantha Wickramasena, who expressed heartfelt gratitude to everyone whose dedication and support made the grand event a resounding success.

title: From Sri Lankan village to Dubai doorstep: Lankan Cart opens Gulf route for small producers | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 21 October 2026 00:06
-     - 7

Lankan Cart, one of the UAE’s established Sri Lankan retail and e-commerce brands, celebrated its seventh anniversary in Dubai with a relaunch under new management and plans to take Sri Lankan products, small producers, and home-grown brands to a wider regional market.

The event, held at LankanCart’s Al Nahda outlet, brought together founders, community leaders, business representatives, Sri Lankan artists and wellwishers. 

Founders Channa and Dilini Munasinghe joined Managing Director Himali Francisco and the new LankanCart team for the occasion, which also saw the launch of the company’s new digital platform.

Under Francisco’s leadership, supported by her husband Sampath Perera, LankanCart is being repositioned from a community retail outlet into a platform connecting Sri Lankan farmers, small producers, entrepreneurs and brands with consumers and businesses in the UAE and, in time, the wider Gulf.

Village life to the doorstep

Addressing the gathering, Francisco said the new team had brought fresh ideas to the business, with the aim of bringing Sri Lanka, and Sri Lankan village life, to the doorstep of every Sri Lankan expatriate in the UAE.

Sampath Perera echoed that vision, saying the goal was to give Sri Lankans everywhere the chance to get the products they want, when they want them, from anywhere in the world. He added that the company also wants to help small producers by making sure that anything Sri Lankans miss from home is available here.

A community role during COVID-19

LankanCart had only recently opened when the COVID-19 pandemic brought normal life in the UAE to a standstill. With movement restricted and many Sri Lankans facing hardship, the Sri Lanka Business Council UAE (SLBC UAE), Sahana and other community partners worked with LankanCart to distribute essential food parcels to Sri Lankan families across the Emirates.

The contribution of SLBC UAE, Sahana and other partners during that period was formally recognised at the anniversary celebration. The experience helped establish LankanCart as a community brand rather than a purely commercial venture.

Space to grow

Chief Guest SLBC UAE Chairman Suren Swaminathan, who attended with his wife Tushara, said the business filled a clear need in the market.

“There are some 350,000 Sri Lankan expatriates in the UAE. There is room for improvement, and there is space for everyone to compete,” he said. “But this is the first time someone has stepped forward to do it this way, while also helping the small farmer in Sri Lanka to get every product out to the market.”

Swaminathan said the new team was driven by passion rather than profit alone, adding that such commitment was essential for the venture to succeed.

From rural Sri Lanka to Gulf consumers

The new management intends to work increasingly with farmers, rural producers, small businesses, women entrepreneurs and emerging brands in Sri Lanka directly, rather than relying solely on conventional import channels. The aim is to give these producers access to an overseas market, better value for their products and a source of foreign exchange.

Through its relaunched website, LankanCart will offer Sri Lankan groceries, fresh vegetables and fruit, spices, snacks and household products for delivery across the UAE. It also plans a business to business platform to support small Sri Lankan businesses.

Expansion plans

Perera has for many years promoted Sri Lanka to overseas investors and business partners. While Francisco leads the day to day growth of the business, the couple see LankanCart as creating benefits at both ends of the supply chain.

The management aims to establish a presence across all seven Emirates, followed by expansion into other Gulf markets, potentially through a franchise model. Its longer term ambitions extend to exports and to promoting Sri Lankan food, culture, heritage and tourism to an international audience.

Representatives of Sahana, SriLankan Airlines, PIMA and other community and business organisations also attended.

Seven years after starting as a small community venture, LankanCart now aims to become a bridge between the Sri Lankan producer and the Gulf consumer, and between Sri Lankans abroad and the tastes of home.

title: David Pieris Group strengthens compliance and  good practices among product and services providers | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 21 October 2026 00:04
-     - 2

David Pieris Group (DPG), one of Sri Lanka’s leading diversified conglomerates, continues to strengthen its commitment to responsible business practices by investing in the development and awareness of its key product and services providers. As part of this ongoing commitment, the group organised an Awareness, Compliance and DPG Good Practices for approximately 70 outsourced service providers, including company owners and responsible representatives.

With a presence across multiple sectors, DPG recognises that maintaining high standards across its operations requires strong collaboration with its product and services providers and business partners. The program was organised as part of DPG’s efforts to take its product and services providers relationships and operational standards to the next level, by enhancing awareness, strengthening accountability and promoting a shared culture of compliance, quality, safety and sustainability.

The program focused on strengthening participants’ understanding of the legal, statutory, contractual and operational responsibilities associated with providing services to DPG. It also provided a common platform to communicate DPG’s expectations relating to compliance, quality, health and safety, environmental management, human resources, security, finance and administration, sustainability and other workplace requirements.

Key areas covered during the program included labour laws and wages board requirements, legal responsibilities of contractors, environmental and waste management, human resources practices, health and safety, security requirements, workers’ compensation insurance (WCI), sustainability and finance and administration requirements.

A panel discussion further enhanced the program by providing participants with an opportunity to clarify important issues, share experiences and exchange views on practical workplace requirements.

The initiative marks another step in David Pieris Group’s ongoing journey to elevate its product and services providers partnerships and build a stronger culture of compliance, quality, safety, sustainability and responsible business practices across its ecosystem.

title: The role of economic science in an era of global power dynamics | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 21 October 2026 00:25
-     - 24

If I were asked whether economic science, as it stands today, could play a positive role in an era of global uncertainty and structural crisis, my answer would be that it is unlikely to do so in its present form. Why do I say this? Let me begin with an anecdote.

In 2008, at the height of the global financial crisis, Queen Elizabeth II visited the London School of Economics (LSE), an institution widely regarded as one of the leading centres of modern economic thought. The Queen reportedly asked a group of distinguished economists: “What actually caused this crisis?” Their answer was that the crisis had been caused by a stochastic shock. The Queen’s response was reportedly one of bewilderment: “What?”

This anecdote captures something fundamental about the crisis of contemporary economic science. If economists cannot adequately explain a major crisis of capitalism in terms that are both intelligible and theoretically meaningful, can we reasonably expect their discipline to play an affirmative role in addressing the structural crises of our time?

Several leading economists have attributed this predicament to the excessive use of mathematics in economic analysis. Let us consider the criticisms of a few prominent economists.

Richard G. Lipsey, author of one of the most widely used economics textbooks, observed:

“To get an article published in most of today’s top rank economic journals, you must provide a mathematical model, even if it adds nothing to your verbal analysis.”

Milton Friedman, a leading figure in monetarism, was also critical of the direction taken by modern economic theory. He argued:

“Economics has become increasingly an archaic branch of mathematics rather than dealing with real economic problems.”

Mark Blaug offered an even more devastating assessment: “Modern economics is sick. Economics has increasingly become an intellectual game play for its own sake and not for its practical consequences for understanding the economic world. Economists have converted the subject into a social mathematics in which analytical rigor is everything and practical relevance is nothing.”

Can the crisis of contemporary economic theory be attributed simply to the excessive mathematisation of the discipline? Or is this tendency a necessary consequence of the social sciences’ persistent attempt to emulate the methods of physics—a phenomenon often described as physics envy? Although these tendencies reinforce one another, I would argue that the fundamental problem lies in the mistaken ontological assumptions underlying mainstream economics—in other words, its conception of the social world that it seeks to explain.

How, then, does mainstream economics conceptualise the social realm?

Let us turn to Frank Hahn, one of the leading contributors to general equilibrium theory, alongside Kenneth Arrow and Gérard Debreu. In his Jevons Memorial Lecture, Hahn acknowledged the centrality of three fundamental propositions in the dominant tradition of economic theory. The first is an atomistic conception of the individual, grounded in methodological individualism, in which individuals are understood as rational agents pursuing their objectives. The second is the proposition that interactions among rational individuals can generate an optimal solution. The third is that, although such an optimum may rarely be realised in practice, the commitment to it remains theoretically essential.

This framework makes it relatively easy for economic theory to emulate the methods of physics. From within this perspective, mathematisation is not merely possible; it becomes almost imperative. Once the economy is conceptualised in terms of individual agents, their optimising behaviour, and the equilibrium outcomes of their interactions, mathematical modelling appears to offer the most appropriate means of analysis.


The problem, however, is not mathematics itself. It is the nature of the assumptions upon which mathematical models are constructed and the relationship between those assumptions and the real world.

From this perspective, the Queen’s reported question becomes particularly revealing. What, precisely, does the concept of a stochastic shock explain? In standard neoclassical modelling, stochastic shocks can encompass a range of disturbances that are not generated endogenously within the model. These may include market imperfections, policy interventions by the state, and natural or human-made disasters. The crucial point is that such disturbances are often treated as external to the model’s underlying economic mechanisms. Consequently, the dominant neoclassical framework struggles to provide a satisfactory account of crises that emerge endogenously from the normal operation of capitalism itself. Its limitations become particularly evident when we seek to explain recurrent financial crises, structural instability, and the contradictory dynamics of capitalist accumulation.

How, then, can we overcome these limitations and make economic science a more useful instrument for understanding and addressing the crises of our time?

I would argue that this requires a Kuhnian paradigm shift in economics, understood as a human and social science. In this presentation, I shall identify two proposed theoretical turns that could contribute to such a transformation: the ontological turn advocated by the British economist Tony Lawson and the classical turn advanced by the late Anwar Shaikh. Let me briefly discuss each in turn.

The classical turn

Anwar Shaikh describes his intellectual journey away from mainstream economic theory in the following terms:

“[T]he standard theory made no sense to me. Utility maximising, optimising, rational expectations, perfect competition just didn’t seem to me explain or even represent the world.

So, I became involved in trying to consider some other foundations. And that lead me to read Joan Robinson and then Luigi Pasinetti, both Cambridge economists, and then from there, to go back to Marx and Smith and Ricardo. And as I did that I began to see that there was in this alternate tradition a way forward, one that began from a completely different beginning, which is how people actually behave, and from that one could derive all the basic tools of micro, and then talking about how economies behave, and having a macro story. But all the story had to be fit together and be consistent from one level to the other. And had to be consistent with empirical evidence and observations on capitalism. That took me a long time, a long, long time. It was a long time because I had to fill gaps.”

The outcome of this intellectual journey was his magnum opus, Capitalism: Competition, Conflict, and Crises.

Shaikh’s work seeks to develop a coherent account of capitalism by grounding microeconomic analysis in the actual behaviour of economic actors and deriving macroeconomic outcomes from the competitive dynamics of the system as a whole. His approach challenges the conventional opposition between microeconomics and macroeconomics by insisting that the two must be theoretically consistent and empirically grounded.

A central element of this framework is his conception of real competition, which differs fundamentally from the idealised model of perfect competition. As Shaikh puts it:

“[Real competition] is completely different from the fiction of perfect competition. Real competition is a war, and competitors use whatever means they can.”

Competition in the real world is therefore not a harmonious process through which markets automatically converge towards an optimal equilibrium. It is a dynamic, conflictual process in which firms struggle for survival, profitability, market share, and competitive advantage. Through this process, economic actors generate outcomes that cannot be adequately understood by treating the economy as a system tending towards equilibrium under conditions of perfect competition.

The classical turn, as developed by Shaikh, thus offers an alternative way of conceptualising the social realm. Rather than beginning with an abstract, hypothetical world of optimising individuals and perfectly competitive markets, it seeks to explain capitalism through the actual behaviour of economic actors, the dynamics of competition, and the systemic tendencies that emerge from their interactions.

This approach also provides a stronger foundation for understanding the endogenous generation of economic crises. Instability and crisis are not necessarily external disturbances imposed upon an otherwise harmonious system. They can emerge from the ordinary workings of capitalist accumulation and competition themselves.

The ontological turn

Tony Lawson’s ontological turn begins from a different, although potentially complementary, point of departure. His primary concern is methodological, but his argument rests on the principle that ontology—the study of the nature of reality—must take precedence over epistemology, the study of how we acquire knowledge of reality.

For Lawson, the central methodological problem in mainstream economics arises from its reliance on mathematical-deductive methods that presuppose closed systems, stable regularities, and specific forms of atomistic interaction. Such methods may be appropriate under certain conditions, but they are inadequate for explaining an open, complex, and changing social reality.

Lawson therefore argues that economic inquiry must begin by examining the nature of the social world itself. This world consists not merely of isolated individuals but also of social relations, institutions, structures, and practices that emerge historically and shape human action. These structures are real, even though they are not always directly observable, and they possess causal powers that cannot be reduced to the actions or intentions of individual agents.

Drawing on Roy Bhaskar’s philosophy of critical realism, Lawson understands social reality as layered and structured. What we observe at the empirical level does not exhaust the reality that generates observable events. A proper explanation must therefore move beyond appearances to investigate the underlying structures, mechanisms, and relations that produce them. As Marx famously observed, if the essence of things and their appearance directly coincided, science would be superfluous.

Critical realism consequently challenges the idea that knowledge can be developed through induction or deduction alone. Instead, it emphasises retroduction: a mode of reasoning that asks what underlying structures, mechanisms, or relations must exist for a particular phenomenon to occur. Through this process, researchers move from observed events towards an explanation of the deeper causal mechanisms that generate them.

The ontological turn therefore calls for a fundamental reorientation of economic science. Rather than imposing predetermined mathematical structures upon the economy, economists must investigate the nature of the economic reality they seek to explain and select their methods accordingly. The objective is not to abandon mathematics, but to ensure that mathematical techniques serve substantive explanation rather than dictate its terms.

Towards a synthesis: Making economic science relevant again

I propose that integrating Shaikh’s classical turn with Lawson’s ontological turn could provide a fruitful foundation for reconstructing economic science as a more powerful instrument for understanding the social world.

Shaikh’s contribution lies in his reconstruction of classical political economy, particularly its account of competition, accumulation, conflict, and crisis. By grounding economic theory in the actual dynamics of capitalism, he offers an alternative to the idealised assumptions of mainstream neoclassical economics.

Lawson’s contribution lies in his insistence that economic explanation must be grounded in an adequate understanding of social reality. His ontological approach draws attention to the structures, institutions, relations, and causal mechanisms that shape economic processes and cannot be reduced to the interactions of isolated individuals.

These two approaches are not identical, and their integration would require further theoretical work. Nevertheless, they share an important commitment: economic theory must be answerable to the nature of the real world rather than to the internal requirements of abstract models alone.

In an era characterised by global uncertainty, recurrent economic crises, growing inequalities, ecological breakdown, and geopolitical instability, economic science cannot fulfil its social responsibility if it remains confined within an abstract framework that struggles to explain the dynamics generating these problems.

What we need is an economic science that combines theoretical rigour with empirical adequacy; that recognises the historically specific and structurally complex nature of capitalism; and that seeks to explain not only how economic systems function, but also why they generate instability, conflict, and crisis.

I therefore conclude that bringing together Shaikh’s classical turn and Lawson’s ontological turn could make a significant contribution to the reconstruction of economic science. Such a reconstruction would help transform economics from an increasingly self-referential mathematical discipline into a socially relevant science capable of explaining the complex realities of our time—and, ultimately, of informing efforts to transform them.

(The author is a retired teacher in Economics. This is a text of the speech presented at the Peradeniya International Economic Research Symposium (PIERS) 2016)

title: Why power cuts again? | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 21 October 2026 00:22
-     - 18

Introduction

Most people associate me with tourism or my interest in wildlife. But before hotels and elephants took over much of my working life, I studied and trained as an electrical power engineer. With several people asking me why we are having power cuts again, I thought I would dust off that old engineering hat and attempt a simple explanation. I will leave the detailed diagnosis to those who operate the system today. But the basic principles have not changed.

What happened on Saturday?

The first thing to understand is that Saturday’s sudden blackout and the scheduled power cuts that followed are two different problems. The blackout occurred when the electricity system lost its balance. The subsequent cuts are being introduced because, with the coal station unavailable, there is insufficient generation available to meet demand during certain hours.

Electricity is rather unforgiving in this respect. At every instant, the amount being generated must closely match the amount being used. We cannot simply produce a little extra in the morning and leave it sitting in the wires until evening. To keep it for later, we need storage.

According to the explanation given by the National System Operator at the Ministry of Energy briefing, the output of Generator No. 1 at Norochcholai suddenly fell from 187 megawatts to less than 5 megawatts at around 11.43 a.m. on 17 October. In ordinary language, the system abruptly lost roughly 185 MW of supply, while consumers were still drawing electricity.

When this happens, the remaining generators initially take the strain and begin to slow. The electrical frequency, normally maintained around 50 hertz, falls. Other generators must respond quickly, or some demand must be disconnected automatically. If the imbalance is not arrested, more generating units can disconnect to protect themselves, making matters worse until the system collapses. That is the broad mechanism of a cascading blackout. The investigation must establish the exact sequence in this case.

Losing one generating unit should normally be a disturbance the system can survive. Power systems are designed to allow for this. Equipment can fail but the rest of the system must be prepared for that possibility. So identifying the first unit that lost output is only part of the explanation. We also need to know why the available reserves and protective control mechanisms did not contain the failure.

Different sources, different limitations

Our electricity comes from a mixture of sources, each with its own strengths and limitations. Norochcholai has three coal-fired units of 300 MW each, giving it a nameplate capacity of 900 MW, with about 810 MW used as its net capacity in planning. This accounts for almost 1/3 of our generating capacity. Therefore it is evident that we are very dependent on the coal plant for our base load requirements. 

We also have a substantial hydroelectric capacity, oil-fired engines and turbines, and growing solar and wind generation. These are not interchangeable machines that can all be switched on and off in the same way. The generation sources for 1 October 2026 is shown in the graph. 

Coal is generally suited to supplying a steady block of electricity over prolonged periods at low cost. A coal station is a large steam-producing system where water must be heated, steam generated, and the turbine brought up to speed and loaded carefully. It is not like starting a diesel generator at the flick of a switch.  A brief trip in the coal generation system can sometimes permit a hot restart, but faults, inspections and restoration procedures can keep a unit out for days. In this instance, the entire station is expected to remain unavailable for several days.

Oil-fired engines and some gas turbines can respond much more quickly. The downside is the cost of fuel. They are useful for meeting peaks and filling gaps, but extensive replacement of coal generation with oil is expensive.

Hydro is particularly valuable because reservoir stations can change output quickly. However, the water in a reservoir is a finite stock. Its use today affects what remains for tomorrow, and some reservoirs also have irrigation and other obligations. Rainfall determines how that stock is replenished. With uncertain weather and the risks posed by climate change, we cannot operate as though the next rains are guaranteed to arrive on schedule.

What replaced the coal?

The figures for two recent Sundays show what happened when coal disappeared. On 11 October, coal supplied 29.4% of the day’s electricity and oil only 0.8%. On 18 October, coal supplied nothing, while oil’s share rose to 23.7%. Hydro, including mini hydro, supplied 52.4%, and solar contributed 22.2%. The system was being kept supplied through a very different combination of sources, with much greater dependence on oil and water.

Why more solar is only part of the answer

People understandably ask why we cannot simply install more solar panels. Solar is useful because it reduces imported fuel consumption and can allow operators to save reservoir water during daylight for use in the evening. But panels generate according to sunlight, rather than according to when we switch on our appliances. After sunset, their direct contribution disappears, just as households are switching on lights, cooking and adding to the evening demand.

On a sunny Sunday or public holiday, the opposite difficulty can arise. Industrial and commercial demand is lower, while solar output may be strong. Operators must reduce other generation or limit some solar output. Coal units cannot be turned down indefinitely, and shutting them down creates another set of problems as explained earlier. Taking too many conventional generators offline can also reduce the system’s ability to absorb sudden disturbances, unless other equipment supplies the necessary support. This does not make solar a bad technology. It means the rest of the electricity system must be developed alongside it.

There is another complication on such days. Solar output can fall quickly when cloud cover moves across an area. Consumers continue using electricity, so other sources must promptly make up the difference. When many solar installations are spread across the country, these local changes tend to smooth one another out. But cloud cover affecting a large concentration of panels can cause a substantial drop. On a low-demand weekend, when fewer conventional generators may be running, there may be less immediate support available. Batteries and responsive hydro can help bridge that gap. Passing clouds should be a manageable operating condition, but without sufficient fast response they can add to the risk of instability. This is a general operating challenge.

Storing electricity for when we need it

Storage helps connect these two situations: electricity available at midday and electricity needed after sunset. Batteries can store energy and return it later. Properly configured, they can also respond very quickly when frequency begins to fall, but their size and operating arrangements matter. Our current available battery fleet (Battery Energy Storage System BESS) is only around 30 MW, as indicated in the figures being discussed, that is about 1% of a 2,800 MW evening peak. 

We must also ask how long the batteries can deliver their output. A 30 MW battery capable of operating for one hour is quite different from a 30 MW battery capable of operating for four. Announcing megawatts without stating the storage duration leaves out half the story. Larger schemes are being procured, but a project on a procurement list cannot supply electricity tonight.

Pumped storage: Old idea still waiting

Then there is pumped storage, an idea Sri Lanka has discussed for years. It is fairly straightforward where electricity is used when it is plentiful to pump water from a lower reservoir to a higher one. When demand rises, release the water back through turbines to generate electricity. Some energy is lost in the process, but we gain the ability to use the remainder when it is more valuable.

JICA-supported pumped-storage planning studies were undertaken in 2013–2015, and CEB’s generation plan identifies a 600 MW Maha Oya scheme with storage for about six hours at full output. The need was recognised well over a decade ago. These projects require substantial investment, environmental assessment and construction time, but those requirements make timely decisions more necessary. So we are still talking about the pumped storage scheme.

Why the power cuts continue

For the public, the immediate answer is therefore fairly simple. Saturday’s blackout began with a sudden loss of generation that the system failed to contain. The evening power cuts that followed are intended to reduce demand while a major source of supply (the coal plant) remains unavailable. Disconnecting selected areas in a controlled manner is a way of avoiding another uncontrolled collapse, until the coal plant can be re-started.

There is no single machine that will solve all these problems. We need dependable generation, well-managed water reserves, adequate storage and controls that can contain a sudden failure. Consumers can help by moving suitable activities into daylight hours, encouraged by sensible tariffs. But responsibility for matching generation investment with the equipment and reserves needed to operate it securely rests with those planning and managing the system.

The consumer should not have to understand any of this to expect a reliable supply. For those responsible for providing it, however, counting the megawatts installed is insufficient. They must know what can actually be delivered on a dry evening, how quickly help will arrive when a unit fails, and how long that help can last.

Notes

title: Why small faults are causing nationwide power failures | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 21 October 2026 00:21
-     - 14

A tree, a relay setting, a 

monkey on a transformer: The triggers are almost 

always trivial. The reason whole 

countries go dark is what the grid fails 

to do next

At about 11:45 on Saturday morning, Sri Lanka’s electricity grid stopped. The National System Operator called it a total system failure; all three generators at the Norochcholai coal plant were reported to have shut down, water plants went offline and mobile and internet services faltered. Power returned in stages, and the operator said supply was fully restored later the same day.

What caused it is not yet known. The Energy Minister, Anura Karunathilaka, said a breakdown at the Upper Kotmale hydropower station was suspected. No official investigation has reported, and no one has said why a fault at a single plant should be able to take down an entire island.

That last question is the real one, and Sri Lanka is not the only country asking it.

The same story, told on every continent

Investigators who have picked through the world’s biggest blackouts keep finding the same shape. In August 2003, tree contact on power lines in Ohio left about 50 million people in the United States and Canada without power. The task force that studied it blamed poor awareness among operators, inadequate tree trimming and failed monitoring at the utility involved.

Six weeks later Italy went dark after two tree flashovers on Swiss lines. Operators did not realise how little time they had, and once Italy split from the rest of Europe, 62 generating units tripped at once and frequency collapsed within about two and a half minutes.

In Turkey in 2015, four long transmission lines were already out for work when a protective relay, set in a way operations staff did not know about, tripped a key line. Generators disconnected when the rules said they should not. In South Australia in 2016, a storm caused repeated voltage dips, wind farms cut output because of a control setting, and the link to the rest of the grid then tripped. About 850,000 customers lost power.

The most thoroughly studied recent case is Iberia. When Spain and Portugal blacked out in April 2025, the European grid body ENTSO-E found no single culprit. Its final report, published in March 2026, describes weak voltage control, oscillations and generators disconnecting early, and says the defences were unable to prevent the collapse.

In each case the first fault was ordinary. In each, the system had little room left to absorb it.

Why a grid has nowhere safe to put a fault

Engineers run grids to a rule known as N-1 security. “N” is the full set of power lines, transformers and generators in service, and “minus one” means the grid must keep working normally if any one of them suddenly fails. Think of a bridge designed so that losing a single cable does not bring it down. Under N-1, operators keep enough spare capacity, and enough alternative routes for electricity, that the loss of one big generator or one major line is an inconvenience, not a catastrophe. The investigations show how that safety margin quietly disappears.

Margins are spent on maintenance. Turkey and continental Europe in 2006 both lost their margin because lines were taken out of service for planned work, leaving the system exposed to the next fault.

Settings hide in the fine print. Relay thresholds, wind-farm control logic and inverter trip points decide whether a plant rides through a disturbance or walks away from it. In several blackouts, the people running the grid did not know what those settings were. A paper hosted by the Asian Development Bank on the February 2025 blackout reported that 11% of 1,608 sampled solar inverters were set to trip at 49.5 hertz rather than the intended 47.

Defences are too slow or too small. When frequency falls faster than automatic load shedding can react, the grid cannot be saved. That is what happened in South Australia, and Turkey’s shedding, even at full capacity, was not enough.

Modern grids are lighter on their feet. Spinning turbines give a grid inertia, a built-in resistance to sudden change. Rooftop solar and wind add clean energy but not inertia, so frequency can move much faster after a loss. Sri Lanka has added more than 1,000 megawatts of rooftop solar since 2018, while its automatic load-shedding scheme was last updated in 2018, according to the same paper.

In short, a fault needs somewhere safe to go. When margins, settings and defences are not right, it goes everywhere.

Sri Lanka has been told what to fix

Saturday was not the island’s first total blackout. Documented islandwide failures include August 2020, late 2021, December 2023 and February 2025, and reports differ on some dates and durations.

The 2020 failure began with a fault during maintenance at Kerawalapitiya, when a safety interlock had been bypassed. A ministry committee found that maintenance protocols recommended after earlier blackouts in 2009 and 2015 had never been put in place. A committee on the 2021 events recommended an auxiliary power supply and a review of relay settings.

The February 2025 blackout, reportedly triggered by a monkey touching a transformer at Panadura, produced a dispute. The Ceylon Electricity Board’s expert panel blamed low system inertia from heavy solar output. The regulator, the Public Utilities Commission, declined to accept that report, held a public hearing and in February 2026 issued directions covering inverter settings, reserve generation, adaptive load shedding and a restoration manual.

Those directions carry no deadlines and no penalties. Several themes, including auxiliary power, relay settings, maintenance and restoration procedures, recur across the committee findings and the 2026 directions. We found no public report on whether they were carried out. That does not prove they were not, but it is the question Saturday’s inquiry will have to answer.

The institutional ground is also shifting. A new Electricity Act is splitting the State utility into successor companies, including the National System Operator and a transmission company, but the market for ancillary services, the reserves and fast responses that stabilise a grid, is not yet established. The then Energy Minister and the ministry secretary resigned in April, and the system operator had already had to cut rooftop solar output and some feeders on days in May and June because of imbalances.

What actually prevents a repeat

No expert quoted in the official reports promises an end to blackouts. After 2003 the US-Canada task force itself said it was impossible to guarantee that large blackouts would never recur. The realistic goals are fewer events, smaller ones and faster recovery.

The measures with the best documentary support are these:

Keep real N-1 security, including during planned outages, with online monitoring that checks continuously whether the grid could survive losing its next line or generator.

Audit protection and inverter settings regularly and test that plants stay connected during disturbances, as the rules require.

Build fast, layered load shedding sized for today’s low-inertia grid. After its 2015 blackout Turkey expanded automatic shedding to 41 per cent of peak load.

Add voltage and frequency support, such as batteries and dynamic reactive power. Ireland now allows up to 75% of its instantaneous power to come from wind and solar, using procured grid services.

Fit disturbance recorders so investigators can establish causes. Missing data limited both the Iberian and earlier Sri Lankan inquiries.

Test black start, the ability to restart a dead grid, under realistic conditions.

The governance lesson may matter more. After 2003 the United States made reliability standards mandatory with penalties, and the energy department tracked all 46 recommendations one by one. Europe’s Iberia inquiry used a panel led by experts from unaffected operators and published findings in stages. By contrast, Argentina’s regulator had reportedly issued no fines a year after its 2019 blackout, and Chile’s critics say no one has been held accountable for February 2025.

Independent proof that any single reform prevents repeats is thin. Much of the evidence is self-reported by the bodies that adopted the reforms, and Italy’s 2003 blackout was followed by a Europe-wide one in 2006. Whatever Sri Lanka adopts after Saturday, the evidence argues for publishing an independent inquiry, setting dated and enforceable obligations, and reporting publicly on whether they are met.

The suspect at Upper Kotmale may yet be confirmed. If it is, that will explain how the blackout began. The inquiry’s harder job is to explain why nothing stopped it.

title: Growth at 4.2%: Real test facing Sri Lanka’s economy | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 21 October 2026 00:20
-     - 13

The claim that political leaders will inevitably lose power if the economy fails to grow should be treated as a serious warning, not an unbreakable rule

The Department of Census and Statistics reports that Sri Lanka’s real GDP grew by 4.2% in the second quarter of 2026, compared with 5.1% in the first quarter. Although the economy continued to grow, the reported rate was lower in the second quarter. The figures have prompted differing views about what this means for the country’s economic and political future. 

In this article, I share my views on the Department’s figures and the comments they have prompted. I consider whether slower economic growth can lead to an economic crisis or political instability. Drawing on Sri Lanka’s latest economic indicators and examples from other countries, I examine how economic difficulties can affect public confidence and, in turn, political stability.

Economic analyst Dhananath Fernando has warned that political leaders may seek to consolidate control over the judiciary, state institutions and other centres of political power. But if they fail to grow the economy and improve people’s lives, they may eventually lose power. This is an important warning. Yet the relationship between economic growth, people’s wellbeing and political power is not automatic. These factors influence one another in complex ways.

What the growth figures tell us

According to the Department, Sri Lanka’s real GDP grew by 4.2% in the second quarter of 2026 compared with the same period in 2025. In the first quarter, growth was 5.1% compared with the same quarter a year earlier. The reported rate was therefore 0.9 percentage points lower in the second quarter. This indicates that the pace of year-on-year growth eased and deserves attention. It does not mean that the economy contracted or is collapsing. Since both figures compare a quarter with the same quarter of the previous year, they cannot, on their own, show whether the economy shrank from one quarter to the next.

The IMF’s forecast also needs to be considered. In May 2026, the IMF said Sri Lanka’s economy had grown by 5% in 2025 and projected growth of 3% for 2026. It identified higher oil prices, conflict in the Middle East and lower tourism receipts as risks to growth and the country’s external finances. The IMF also projected public debt at about 100.1% of GDP in 2026. 

The IMF’s 3% figure and the Department’s 4.2% figure measure different things. The IMF figure is a forecast for the whole of 2026; the Department’s figure measures the change in economic output in the second quarter compared with the same quarter a year earlier. The IMF forecast was also issued before the second-quarter results were published. The two figures should not be treated as directly comparable, or as if one disproves the other. Read together, however, they point to a central challenge: keeping growth on track while protecting the economy from external shocks.

Growth also varied across sectors. In the second quarter, industrial activity expanded by 7.3%, while services grew by 2.7%. Agricultural activity, by contrast, contracted by 2.3%. Growth in construction and mining supported industry, while information technology, financial services and telecommunications contributed to growth in services. However, the Department reported slower growth in some services, including tourism-related activities, than in the same period a year earlier. 

The decline in agriculture deserves particular attention. According to the Department’s figures, value added in rice cultivation fell by 15.1%, while freshwater fishing and aquaculture fell by 61%. Agriculture’s importance cannot be judged only by its share of GDP. A decline in agricultural activity can affect food supplies, farmers’ incomes, rural employment, food prices and the need for imports. It is therefore more than a figure in the national accounts: it can affect rural household incomes and the cost of food for consumers. 

The key question is not only whether GDP is growing. We must also ask whether that growth creates secure, good-quality jobs; raises household incomes after allowing for price increases; and gives small businesses the confidence to invest and expand. If the cost of living remains high, or if the gains from growth reach only a small part of society, people may not feel the improvement shown in the official figures. Public confidence depends not only on the growth rate, but also on whether people experience the benefits of growth in their daily lives.

Lessons from other countries

Sri Lanka’s 2022 crisis is the clearest example of how severe economic hardship can affect political stability. It was not simply a period of slower growth. Foreign exchange shortages, the suspension of debt payments, shortages of fuel and other essential goods, and rising living costs reinforced one another. The World Bank reported that jobs were lost, while food insecurity and poverty increased during the crisis. Shortages and the hardships of daily life contributed to mass protests, and the President resigned. The crisis showed how economic distress can shake political power. But it was a far deeper breakdown than a modest decline in the growth rate: the country faced a debt crisis and a collapse in its ability to pay for imports. 

Argentina’s crisis in 2001 offers another example. As the country’s financial and debt problems worsened, public protests grew. The President resigned, the Government defaulted on its debt, and the exchange-rate system was abandoned. Argentina’s experience shows how an economic crisis can become a crisis of public confidence when people’s incomes, savings and jobs are all under pressure. 

Greece offers a different lesson. A prolonged recession, high unemployment and painful economic adjustment weakened public support for established political parties, while new political forces gained ground. This shows that the way people experience economic policies—and whether they believe the costs are being shared fairly—can shape their political response. Difficult reforms may be necessary, but carrying them out without public trust and support for those most affected can deepen political instability.

Zimbabwe, however, shows that economic decline does not always remove a Government from power. The country experienced prolonged periods of high inflation, currency instability and falling production. Yet restrictions on opposition activity and the concentration of state power helped the ruling party remain in office. Economic failure can increase the risk that a Government will lose power, but it does not guarantee that outcome. Electoral rules, independent institutions, media freedom, the strength of the opposition and people’s ability to organise also matter.

Debt, growth and public confidence

Slower growth can increase debt risks, but debt sustainability depends on more than the growth rate. Interest costs, Government revenue, the budget balance, the maturity of debt, and whether it is owed locally or abroad all matter. The IMF’s 2026 estimate puts public debt at about 100.1% of GDP. Reducing that burden will require growth, stronger public revenue and careful spending to work together. 

Sri Lanka therefore needs more than a higher growth rate. It needs a stronger economic base that can sustain growth over time. This means expanding exports and competitive production, creating a stable environment for private investment, improving agricultural productivity, providing young people with good jobs, and protecting those most affected by economic reforms. If growth is not broad enough to benefit many people, it may appear in the statistics without restoring public confidence.

The claim that political leaders will inevitably lose power if the economy fails to grow should be treated as a serious warning, not an unbreakable rule. Long periods of economic weakness can increase public dissatisfaction, strengthen political opposition and raise the risk of a crisis of Government. Whether this leads to a change in power also depends on the country’s political and institutional conditions.

In the end, leaders must answer a simple question: do people feel the recovery in their incomes, jobs and daily lives, or do they see it only in the statistics? If the answer is no, it will become harder for any Government to retain public confidence—and harder to remain in power.

(The author is Emeritus Professor of Economics, University of Colombo)

title: Accessible tourism: Sri Lanka’s overlooked opportunity to build a competitive visitor experience | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 21 October 2026 00:00
-     - 3

Inclusive Tourism Australia Founder and CEO Melissa James

By Charumini de Silva

Accessible tourism remains one of the industry’s most overlooked opportunities, often misunderstood as an expensive exercise in installing ramps, widening doorways and redesigning facilities for wheelchair users. Yet, the market extends far beyond physical disabilities, including travellers with hearing and visual impairments, mobility limitations and age-related needs, as well as those who simply benefit from more accessible experiences.

For Sri Lanka, the opportunity is both social and commercial. With an ageing global population, longer life expectancy and growing demand for inclusive travel, the ability to accommodate visitors with different needs could help diversify the country’s tourism offering, strengthen competitiveness and encourage repeat visits.

“It’s a large market, and it’s getting bigger,” said Inclusive Tourism Australia Founder and CEO Melissa James, who outlined that businesses do not need to undertake expensive transformations to begin making a difference.


A qualified access consultant with over 12 years of experience, James works with tourism operators, destination management organisations and governments to identify accessibility barriers and develop practical solutions. Her work spans accessibility assessments, destination reviews, industry training and capacity building. In 2018, she spoke at the World Summit on Accessible Tourism in Brussels on how collaboration between governments, businesses and communities can drive meaningful change.

On her first visit to Sri Lanka, James has been engaging with local tourism suppliers to understand the industry’s opportunities and challenges. She also conducted a training session at Sri Lanka’s first tourism forum dedicated to improving accessibility for visitors with disabilities, organised last week by Australia’s Market Development Facility (MDF) in partnership with Ayu by Walkers Tours.

In an interview with the Daily FT, she discusses the commercial case for accessible tourism, practical steps businesses can take without significant investment, the importance of reliable accessibility information and what Sri Lanka needs to do to turn inclusion into a competitive advantage. Below are excerpts of the interview;

Q: Accessible tourism is both a basic human right and a business opportunity. Why has the industry been slow to recognise its potential?

A: Many operators misunderstand what accessible tourism means. They immediately think of wheelchair users, ramps and wider doors, then conclude that it is too difficult or expensive. But wheelchair users represent only a part of the market. Once operators understand the broader range of people who benefit from accessibility, they begin to recognise the opportunity. 

Another major barrier is simply not knowing where to start. If businesses are given practical ideas and shown what they can do immediately, they become more willing to act. 

I always say this is not a sprint; it is a marathon. Accessibility takes time, and businesses do not need to transform everything overnight. They can begin with small, affordable changes that make a meaningful difference. 

A restaurant, for instance, can provide large-print menus with dark text on a light background. A hotel that already has a step-free shower and a handheld shower head could provide a shower chair. For someone with mobility difficulties who does not use a wheelchair, that simple addition could make the room suitable for their needs.

There are many improvements businesses can make quickly, without substantial financial or physical investment.

Q: How significant is the accessible travel market, and what are businesses missing by failing to cater to it?

A: It is estimated that 24% of international travellers require access. Sri Lanka welcomed approximately 2.36 million international visitors last year, so even a quarter of that market represents a substantial opportunity.

The market is also growing as people live longer and the global population ages. 


Many older travellers have the financial means and the desire to travel, but may experience back pain, knee problems, hearing loss, impaired vision or other conditions that affect their mobility and independence. They still want to enjoy holidays and experiences like everyone else. Better accessibility allows them to do so more comfortably and confidently.

Businesses that overlook this market are missing potential customers. Those that understand their needs can improve their offerings, attract new visitors and encourage repeat business.

Q: In most destinations, accessibility is often reduced to ramps and wheelchair access. What does genuinely inclusive tourism look like in practice?

A: Access is about infrastructure; can you get someone there? Inclusion is about ensuring that, once there, they can participate in the experience. 

A good example is the Yala safari jeep, which we have discussed since I arrived in Sri Lanka. A wheelchair user might be accommodated in the front seat beside the driver, while their friends and family sit in the back. The person can go on the safari, but they are separated from their group. That is access without meaningful inclusion.

We need to consider how everyone can share the experience rather than simply get through the door.

Similarly, a beach wheelchair mat may enable someone to reach the water’s edge, but what happens next? Can they get into the water and enjoy the experience alongside everyone else?

That is the distinction. Accessibility provides the means to participate; inclusion ensures people can enjoy the whole experience together.

Q: For businesses operating on tight margins, what practical improvements can they make without major investment?

A: The first step is to document what they already offer through an access statement. This should explain the facilities available, the barriers that remain and the type of visitor the business can accommodate.

Businesses can also improve printed materials by using larger fonts and clearer layouts, then identify ways to build on their existing facilities.


For example, a hotel with a step-free room, a step-free shower and a handheld shower head could add a shower chair. That relatively small investment may make the room suitable for people who cannot stand for long periods.

Businesses cannot cater to absolutely everybody, and they do not have to. They need to understand whom they can accommodate, communicate that clearly and focus on the market they can serve well. 

There are also simple ways to make tourism experiences more inclusive. Consider a whale-watching operator. Laminated information cards identifying the marine life visitors might see, with descriptions of each species, would help deaf or hard-of-hearing visitors who cannot access the spoken commentary. These are small changes, but they can significantly improve the overall experience.

Q: How important is accessibility information in helping travellers plan and book with confidence?

A: It is essential. Travellers need accurate, practical information to determine whether a destination, accommodation provider or activity will meet their individual needs.

Everyone’s disability and abilities are different. Someone might be able to walk along a flat path but struggle to climb stairs without a handrail. A hotel does not necessarily need a completely flat entrance to accommodate that person, provided it has suitable steps and handrails. The important thing is to explain what is available and allow travellers to make informed decisions.

Service providers should conduct an access audit, document their findings and publish the information on their websites, ideally supported by photographs. Travellers research extensively before booking, and they need to know what to expect. Research cited in the industry indicates that 86% of travellers want better practical accessibility information. If one business provides that information, while its competitors do not, it has an advantage.

Technology can make this information easier to access and use, but the foundation must be accurate, detailed and transparent information. Businesses should not simply label themselves accessible; they should explain precisely what visitors can and cannot do.

Q: What would it take for Sri Lanka to turn accessible tourism into a competitive advantage?

A: Sri Lanka has already started making progress, and some operators are doing good work. The next step is to connect those efforts and create itineraries that allow travellers to plan complete trips.

You could have the most accessible hotel in the world, but if visitors cannot access attractions, activities or experiences around it, the overall destination is still limited. Hotels, tour operators, accommodation providers and experience operators need to work together to understand what each can offer and how those services can be combined into inclusive itineraries.

Walkers Tours, for example, has itineraries in place and understands which accommodation providers offer different levels of accessibility. It has also partnered with experience providers willing to accommodate visitors with disabilities.

We visited a whale-watching operation where the boat itself was not wheelchair-accessible, but the staff’s attitude helped overcome that barrier. They were willing to assist wheelchair users to board, and the operator is now considering simple modifications, including a platform that would allow seated visitors to see over the railings. That is encouraging. The operator is identifying what can be improved rather than dismissing the opportunity because the boat is not fully accessible.

Clear communication remains essential. If a wheelchair user cannot board independently but trained crew members can assist, the access statement should explain that. Visitors can then decide whether the arrangement meets their needs.

Independent verification by qualified access consultants can also build confidence. When a business’s accessibility claims have been assessed, travellers have a stronger basis for choosing that experience, while operators can benefit from increased trust and repeat visits.

Q: What are the government’s priorities in ensuring accessibility becomes part of Sri Lanka’s tourism development rather than remaining a voluntary initiative?

A: As far as I understand, Sri Lanka is looking at developing accessibility standards. During my visit, I am scheduled to meet representatives of the Sri Lanka Tourism Development Authority (SLTDA) and the relevant qualifications body to discuss the development of standards, alongside training pathways through which people can become qualified and certified.

The response from Government representatives at the recent workshop was encouraging. There appeared to be genuine interest in exploring what could be implemented and how the industry could move forward.

Establishing clear standards is important, but so is developing the expertise needed to assess compliance and help businesses understand what is required.

Q: What lessons can Sri Lanka draw from Australia’s approach to accessibility standards and implementation?

A: In Australia, accessibility requirements are incorporated into the National Construction Code, meaning new buildings must comply with the applicable standards. Compliance is considered throughout the construction process. Certifiers assess buildings at different stages, and a final inspection is required before an occupation certificate is issued. Accessibility therefore needs to be considered from the planning and design stages, rather than treated as an afterthought.

There is also a growing role for qualified access consultants in development applications submitted to local councils. Some councils require consultants to review plans and confirm whether they comply with accessibility requirements.

Sri Lanka could consider a similar approach once its standards are established, ensuring that accessibility is incorporated into the design and construction of new buildings. The Gold Coast offers a useful illustration. It has been a tourism destination for decades, so many older buildings remain. However, newer hotels and apartment buildings must comply with current requirements, expanding the accommodation options available to travellers who need accessible facilities.


The key lesson is to build accessibility into development from the beginning. Retrofitting existing buildings can be challenging, but ensuring new developments meet appropriate standards can steadily expand the supply of accessible accommodation.

Q: Beyond construction standards, how should destinations measure whether their tourism industries are becoming genuinely inclusive?

A: Destinations need to work with qualified access consultants and embed accessibility into their broader planning and decision-making.

In Australia, I worked with Bellingen Shire Council to develop an inclusive tourism strategic plan. The council adopted it as part of its business development strategy, meaning future decisions must take the plan into account. The approach has also helped the area secure Federal Government funding for accessibility-related infrastructure.

Accessibility can be incorporated into procurement policies, too. Consider taps and door handles: lever-operated designs are easier for people with hand-mobility difficulties to use. A council or business can require these fittings whenever replacements are made. That is how change becomes embedded in everyday decisions. It does not always require a separate, expensive project; sometimes it means making accessibility a standard consideration whenever something is built, purchased or upgraded.

Destinations should also assess whether visitors can access a complete experience, from accommodation and transport to attractions, activities and information. Counting ramps or accessible rooms alone will not tell the whole story.

Q: How can Sri Lanka raise awareness of inclusive tourism and position itself as a destination for travellers with disabilities?

A: Raising awareness is key. Sri Lanka could work with its para-athletes, including those who compete internationally, to create ambassador roles and help make accessibility more visible.

As businesses become more aware of the opportunity, interest can grow organically. Sustainability was once seen as an additional responsibility, but it has increasingly become part of how tourism businesses operate. Accessibility can follow a similar path.

There are already encouraging examples in Sri Lanka. At DoubleTree by Hilton, we were shown accessible accommodation, and the team explained that its accessible rooms attract repeat visits from domestic travellers who know what facilities are available. That is a powerful message. Businesses do not necessarily need to wait for international visitors to recognise the opportunity; domestic tourism can also generate demand.

Sri Lanka has a substantial domestic visitor base, alongside its international arrivals. Making tourism experiences more accessible can help more people enjoy the country’s attractions and encourage visitors to return. The industry needs to communicate what is available, be honest about limitations and make it easier for travellers to identify experiences suited to their needs.

Q: Having spent a week engaging with Sri Lanka’s tourism industry, what is your overall assessment of its readiness to move forward?

A: I am excited by what is already happening in Sri Lanka. I was particularly encouraged by the interest shown during the training session and by the discussions among government representatives about what could be implemented and what needs to be considered.

There is momentum, and the challenge now is to maintain it. The industry does not need to solve everything at once. It needs to start with practical improvements, share information, build partnerships and progressively strengthen standards and skills.

I would be very happy to return and contribute to that process.
